classification.difficultyReason: Part b requires selecting overlapping right triangles with common hypotenuse BC, applying RHS, and transferring matching angles to the outer triangle before using the isosceles converse.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use congruence to prove that $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with angle bisector AR and a right angle at R; ordinary source blue strokes use house black.
spec.mathematics: B, R, C are collinear; AR is perpendicular to BC; angle BAR equals angle RAC.

answer.short: $\triangle ARB\equiv\triangle ARC$ (AAS), so $AB=AC$. Hence $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.
answer.worked:
In triangles $ARB$ and $ARC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAR&=\angle CAR &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ARB&=\angle ARC=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular lines)}\\AR&=AR &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ARB\equiv\triangle ARC$ (AAS). Hence $AB=AC$ (matching sides of congruent triangles), so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use congruence to prove that $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, given that $BP=CQ$.

spec.description: Crossing perpendicular segments BP and CQ inside triangle ABC; their intersection remains unlabelled.
spec.mathematics: P lies on AC, Q lies on AB, BP is perpendicular to AC, and CQ is perpendicular to AB.
spec.answerVisibility: No congruence conclusion or additional equal-side marks are supplied.

answer.short: $\triangle BQC\equiv\triangle CPB$ (RHS), giving $\angle QBC=\angle PCB$. Thus $AB=AC$ and $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.
answer.worked:
In right-angled triangles $BQC$ and $CPB$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BQC&=\angle CPB=90^\circ &&\text{(given)}\\BC&=CB &&\text{(common hypotenuse)}\\CQ&=BP &&\text{(given)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BQC\equiv\triangle CPB$ (RHS). Hence $\angle QBC=\angle PCB$ (matching angles). Since $Q$ lies on $AB$ and $P$ lies on $AC$, $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. Therefore $AB=AC$ (sides opposite equal angles), so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.
